source: Ashton and Cairney (2021) Future-relevant memories are not selectively strengthened during sleep (PLoS ONE)
finding: Two online direct replications of Wilhelm 2011 found the sleep benefit but no sleep x expectancy interaction. Bayes factors favour the null.
numbers: Exp 1: 230 recruited, 162 analysed (cells 42/39/50/31), 40 word pairs, tests at 12 h and 7 days. 12 h: delay F(1,158)=9.67 p=.002; expectancy F=0.63 p=.428; interaction F=0.07 p=.786, BF01=4.00. 7 d: interaction F=1.34 p=.249, BF01=2.47. Exp 2: 213 recruited, 124 analysed (31/cell, 82 excluded for expectancy mismatch), 100 pairs, 12 h: delay F(1,120)=5.27 p=.023; interaction F=0.45 p=.504, BF01=3.42. Power planned at d=0.86 from Wilhelm.
limits: Online, unsupervised; sleep group was less alert (SSS p<.001); sleep hours self-reported; large exclusion for expectancy mismatch in Exp 2; Wilhelm-sized effect assumed in power.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct replication failure. A test-expectancy tag should not be assumed to change what is kept by an offline pass.

source: Back-of-envelope pooling of test-expectancy x sleep interactions (own calculation from d01, a01, b05, a13)
finding: No published meta-analysis exists (Europe PMC title/abstract searches returned none). A rough Fisher-z pool of five independent interaction tests, with every sign set positive (optimistic), gives a small effect near r=0.10.
numbers: Partial eta2 -> r: Wilhelm Exp1 p=.05 (F about 3.9, N=104) r=.19; Ashton Exp1 12 h r=.02 (N=162); Ashton Exp2 r=.06 (N=124); Wamsley maze r=.10 (N=75); Barner 2023 p=.12 (F about 2.5, N=56) r=.21. Pooled r=0.097, 95% CI [0.010, 0.183], k=5. Script D:/research_scratch/B04.03/tmp/B04.03_pool.py.
limits: NOT a real meta-analysis: F back-calculated from p-values, signs assumed positive (Wamsley distance interaction was opposite, Ashton direction unknown), Barner used within-subject relevance not a between-group expectancy manipulation, no unpublished nulls. Treat as an upper bound.
agent_relevance: Even optimistically the interaction is small (r about 0.1, lower CI near zero). Gap 4 is only partly closed: a formal meta-analysis still needs doing.

source: Petzka, Charest, Balanos and Staresina (2021) Does sleep-dependent consolidation favour weak memories? (Cortex)
finding: Under easy retrieval only weakly encoded memories showed a sleep benefit. Adding retroactive interference at test revealed a sleep benefit for strong memories too, so the weak-memory advantage is partly a ceiling effect.
numbers: 128 tested, 8 excluded (120 analysed), object-sequence Memory Arena, between subjects. No interference: delay main effect F(1,56)=11.59 p=.001 etap2=.17; delay x strength F(1,56)=5.78 p=.020 etap2=.09. Weak: sleep > wake t(26.63)=3.25 p=.003 d=1.19. Strong: t(20.40)=1.11 p=.28 d=.41 BF01=1.82. With interference: weak t(27.61)=2.27 p=.031 d=.83; strong t(27.93)=4.64 p<.001 d=1.70.
limits: One spatial-temporal task, small cells (about 15 per cell), strength set by training criterion not by relevance.
agent_relevance: Weak traces gain more only when tests are easy. For an agent: do not discard weak lessons on strength alone; difficulty of the later task matters.

source: Schabus, Ameen and Heib (2025/2026) Sleep preserves, wake differentiates: strength-dependent forgetting of declarative memories (J Sleep Res 10.1111/jsr.70348; preprint 10.1101/2025.11.03.686279)
finding: Sleep kept weak and strong word pairs equally. Wake caused the loss, and the loss fell mostly on weak pairs. Sleep oscillation measures did not relate to overnight retention.
numbers: 90 adults, n=30 per group (immediate, 9 h sleep with PSG, 9 h wake), 80 word pairs, half seen twice (weak), half three times (strong). Strong > weak in all groups. Wake group lost more weak than strong; sleep group did not differ from immediate recall. No significant SO/spindle/coupling correlation with retention.
quote: sleep protects declarative memories irrespective of initial encoding strength
limits: Abstract read only (via Europe PMC); exact test statistics not seen. Strength was varied by repetition.
agent_relevance: Supports a protect-by-default store: weak lessons are lost by neglect (the wake analogue), not by selective erasure. Weak-but-relevant lessons should be actively kept.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length (arXiv 2506.08184)
finding: An explicit in-context directed-forgetting instruction ('Forget all the previous updates to <key>') did not reduce interference in five LLMs. Errors clustered at the position of the instruction. Only a fake Q&A reset (mock user query, fabricated assistant reply, new task) helped.
numbers: Models tested include gemini-2.0-flash, Llama-4-maverick, gpt-4.1-mini, mistral-small-2503; 46 unique keys, update counts 20-150. Per-key forget < 10 points gain over baseline at 100 updates, negative for gpt-4.1-mini. Forward-focus and relevance meta-prompt also ineffective (harmful for gpt-4.1-mini). Mock QA reset inserted 120 updates before the query gave a substantial but declining gain. Accuracy still falls log-linearly with update count.
quote: natural language instructions--whether to forget or focus--do not effectively reduce interference in LLM retrieval tasks
limits: Synthetic key-value update streams, not agent lessons; only a few prompt wordings; no reasoning models noted in the text read.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on a 'drop' instruction inside the same context. Remove or move the item out of the context instead, or use a hard boundary. Closes gap 10 for the in-context case.

source: Xie (2026) Learning to Forget: SleepGate (arXiv 2603.14517), re-read for baseline and prompt-engineering claims
finding: SleepGate's own motivation is that instructions to ignore old values give only marginal relief; its gain comes from a learned gate on a tiny model. The full-cache baseline reaches only 8.0 percent even at one prior update.
numbers: 4 layers, 793K parameters, 200 episodes per depth. SleepGate 99.5 percent at depth 5, 97.0 percent at 10, 73.5 percent at 15, 16.5 percent at 30. Five baselines (full cache, sliding window, H2O, StreamingLLM, decay-only) at or below 18 percent. Stale retrieval rate 62 percent at n=30. Sleep overhead 15.6 percent.
limits: Toy model trained from scratch on the same synthetic task; baselines get no task-specific gate; no test of a prompted frontier LLM. The prompt-failure claim is cited from d05, not tested here.
agent_relevance: A gate needs training; at agent scale the practical equivalent is explicit removal from context. Does not show that a prompt-only drop works.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents (arXiv 2505.16067), Table 2 re-read from the PDF text
finding: Reconstructed Table 2 (rows paired by memory size, which falls in order none > period > history > combined): history-based deletion helps EHRAgent and CIC-IoT under both evaluators, is flat on AgentDriver under the strict evaluator, hurts AgentDriver and RegAgent under the coarse evaluator, and hurts RegAgent under strict.
numbers: Strict evaluator, none -> history (memory size): RegAgent 70.95 -> 67.65 (2938 -> 949); EHRAgent 38.67 -> 42.06 (1012 -> 784); AgentDriver 51.00 -> 51.81 (1178 -> 846); CIC-IoT 85.40 -> 89.60 (904 -> 788). Combined: 66.58, 42.34, 49.97, 85.50 (sizes 890, 248, 323, 188). Coarse C1 evaluator, none -> history: RegAgent 63.18 -> 60.88; EHRAgent 25.91 -> 33.55; AgentDriver 36.92 -> 34.00; CIC-IoT 74.00 -> 78.10. Periodic deletion (fixed retrieval-count threshold) costs 0 to 4.6 points: CIC-IoT strict 85.40 -> 80.80, coarse 74.00 -> 73.70.
quote: with a reliable utility evaluator, history-based deletion can improve agent performance
limits: Two-column PDF text; pairing of rows is inferred from the memory-size ordering and matches the text description (GPT-4o-mini history evaluator gains on EhrAgent, loses on AgentDriver), but the Figure 5 per-evaluator panels were not viewed. Deletion rule: retrieved at least n times and mean utility of past retrievals below a threshold.
agent_relevance: Outcome-based deletion after at least n retrievals is the nearest thing to a future-use test: it removed 5 to 75 percent of memory without loss on 3 of 4 agents under a strict judge. Needs a reliable judge. Closes gap 9 with moderate confidence.

source: Chen and Cheng (2026) Learning What to Remember (arXiv 2606.12945), full text re-read
finding: Retention is scored as the share of gold-evidence turns kept, not answer accuracy. Learned weights are fit against that same gold-retention label, so the weights show what predicts gold in LongMemEval-S, not what predicts later use in an agent.
numbers: 479 usable LongMemEval-S cases, keep 30 percent. Blind: learned 0.770 +/- 0.011, uniform 0.657, self-relevance 0.518, reliability 0.497, recency 0.368, goal relevance 0.286, emotion 0.201, random 0.300. Bootstrap gaps: +0.120 vs uniform [0.091, 0.149]; +0.402 vs recency [0.350, 0.452]. Oracle: goal relevance 0.979, learned 0.993. Learned weights: reliability 0.64, emotional intensity 0.55, self-relevance 0.23, goal relevance 0.00. MLP over the same factors 0.773 (tie).
limits: Retention proxy, one benchmark, factors are rated by an LLM or heuristics; recency and emotion were worse than random here.
agent_relevance: Best available support that a multi-factor future-use score beats recency, but it uses label-fitted weights. Gap 1 not closed: no test against real reuse.

source: Annapureddy and Thamatani (2026) The Epistemics of Agent Memory (arXiv 2609.33013), full text re-read
finding: A learned promote/forget policy under a token budget got higher task success but forgot load-bearing clusters at chance precision. Adding agent-observable forgetting-evidence features with hindsight regret raised forgetting precision to 0.93 but made the gate almost inactive. Rollback that restores source experiences fixed a poisoned rule.
numbers: Success +22.7 percent relative over the best non-learned baseline (paired CI +1.89 to +11.34 pp), 7.17x compression; forgetting precision 0.319 vs junk base rate 0.333; 74 percent of load-bearing clusters destroyed at least once; 75 percent of a -15.0 pp transfer regression traced to forget -> re-promotion -> poisoning. Raw experience 7.3x/9.4x over budget. Regret-feature variant: precision 0.932 (hard) / 0.833 (medium), but 0.61 forgets per seed vs 30, success regressed; prevalence coupling 0.593 -> 0.388. Rollback fired 5/5 seeds, task success 0.0 -> 1.0.
limits: Synthetic benchmark made by the authors, 10 held-out seeds.
agent_relevance: Evidence for soft/reversible handling: hard forgetting at budget pressure destroys needed items; keeping source and rolling back recovered success. A hindsight-regret signal is a write-after-outcome tag that does predict junk.

source: Li and Li (2026) What Should an Agent Forget? RD-Forget (arXiv 2609.10263), full text
finding: Keeping a source archive and suppressing superseded facts per query, scored on answer accuracy on public benchmarks, beat two experience-memory baselines. Removing the forgetting step cost the most; removing the rescue step (historical eligibility) cost 3.5 to 9 points.
numbers: Five suites (LoCoMo-style AMB-Text, LongMemEval knowledge update, MemoryAgentBench fact consolidation, BEAM, PersonaMem), four backbones. Fact-consolidation gains 11.00 to 26.00 points over the better of ACE and ReasoningBank. Luna ablations (AMB-Text / LME-KU / MAB-FC): matched full 91.86 / 93.59 / 74.00; -FORGET 68.60 / 60.26 / 51.00; -QC 77.91 / 82.05 / 56.00; -RESCUE 88.37 / 91.03 / 65.00; -SLOT 86.05 / 89.74 / 64.00. PersonaMem Qwen 59.93 vs ACE 39.21 and RB 38.17.
limits: Authors' method on public benchmarks; baselines are not forgetting methods; fact-update tasks where forgetting is defined by supersession, not future relevance. Ablations from one backbone (Luna).
agent_relevance: Soft forgetting (suppress, keep source, allow rescue) works on answer accuracy; the rescue path is measurably needed. Partly closes gap 3 (rescue cost measured; hard-delete arm not run) and gap 8 (public benchmarks, accuracy).

source: Rana et al. (2026) OBLIVION (arXiv 2604.00131), results re-read
finding: Decay-driven lowered accessibility plus reinforcement on use matched or slightly beat full-context and flat retrieval on LongMemEval and GoodAI LTM, with large token savings. With the strongest backbone and a large window the full-context agent stayed competitive and the gain was mostly efficiency.
numbers: LongMemEval (S): flat retrieval baseline LME-RFT 89.00 percent with GPT-4.1-mini; OBLIVION reaches 90.60 percent; single-layer M1 86.40 percent. Token reduction up to 73 percent at 120K span. GoodAI LTM normalised sums for GPT-4.1-mini: 9.20 / 8.41 / 6.79 / 6.70 vs 8.53 / 5.37 / 6.68 / 6.26 for a memory baseline.
limits: Authors' method; EverMemOS reproduced by the authors; accuracy gain about 1.6 points on LongMemEval-S.
agent_relevance: Independent benchmarks, answer accuracy: forgetting-as-accessibility is roughly neutral on accuracy and saves tokens. Does not show a clear accuracy gain over keep-all when the window is large.

finding: Adaptive decay with relevance and access signals kept more critical facts at lower storage than baselines on the authors' LTI-Bench, with F1 gains on LoCoMo multi-hop.
numbers: LTI-Bench after 30 simulated days: 82.1 percent critical-fact retention; LoCoMo ablation: removing a component drops multi-hop F1 from 29.43 to 19.45 (33.9 percent), another to 13.63, another to 22.88 (22.4 percent); abstract states 45 percent storage reduction. Compared against Mem0 and others on Multi-Session Chat, LoCoMo and LTI-Bench.
limits: LTI-Bench is the authors' own and scored on retention; LoCoMo F1 is a public benchmark. Short paper (5 pages).
agent_relevance: Mixed: retention proxy on own benchmark, F1 on public one. Not independent evidence of better answers than keep-all.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute (arXiv 2504.13171), section 5.4 and 6 re-read
finding: The gain of precomputing grows as the question becomes more predictable from the context (predictability = log-probability of the question given the context under Llama2-70B base). On a real agentic coding task sleep-time compute helped only at low test-time budgets.
numbers: Stateful GSM-Symbolic P1 and P2 split into five predictability quantiles: accuracy gap between sleep-time and standard test-time compute widens with predictability (shown in Figure 10, bin values not in text). Abstract: up to 13 percent (GSM) and 18 percent (AIME) accuracy gain, about 5x less test-time compute for equal accuracy, 2.5x lower cost per query on Multi-Query GSM. SWE-Features (Claude 3.7 Sonnet): higher F1 at low budgets (roughly 3000-5000 tokens per question) but standard test-time scaling better at higher budgets.
limits: Gap by bin only in a figure; synthetic context-question pairs; no test of lesson distillation.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 7 in part: gain depends on predictability and disappears at high budget. Precompute lessons only for task types the agent will meet again.

source: Kolibius, Born and Feld (2021) Vast amounts of encoded items nullify but do not reverse the effect of sleep on declarative memory (Front Psychol)
finding: Re-read for store-size boundary: with 640 word pairs sleep gave no benefit and no harm. Sleep benefit is a function of load.
numbers: N=78 (38 sleep, 40 wake); wake -11.2 (SEM 1.73) vs sleep -8.5 (SEM 1.70), F(1,74)=1.25 p=.27; equivalence rules out harm beyond d=-0.20; BF01=8.26 against harm.
limits: One task and one load level above the threshold; the below-threshold comparison comes from earlier smaller-load studies, not this paper.
agent_relevance: Only human numeric boundary on store size, so the pruning payoff point for agents (gap 2) has no direct measurement; use the Xiong memory sizes (hundreds to about 3000 records) as the only agent-side range.

source: Reverberi, Kohn and Fernandez (2020) and Wamsley (2016) as summarised by Ashton and Cairney (2021)
finding: Ashton and Cairney summarise the evidence as: Wamsley 2016 no effect of test knowledge on overnight retention for declarative or nondeclarative memory; Reverberi 2020 no effect of explicit relevance instruction on neural correlates of retention after sleep; reward and emotion also mostly null.
numbers: No new numbers; refs 34 and 35 in that paper. Note that Wamsley found an expectation main effect in both sleep and wake.
limits: Secondary characterisation; Ashton's description of Wamsley (no impact) differs from Wamsley's own title and abstract (expectation helps in both).
agent_relevance: Shows the field's own summary of the relevance effect is: instruction effects exist, sleep specificity does not replicate.

source: Search status: no direct test of write-time future-use tags vs real reuse in agent memory (gaps 1 and 6)
finding: The WebSearch quota ran out and arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs returned rate limits, so a fresh literature sweep for 2026 agent papers testing write-time tags against later reuse was NOT possible. Within the papers opened (d05-d14 plus series a-c) none logs whether each stored lesson was later used and correlates a write-time tag with it.
numbers: Closest proxies: Xiong 2025 history-based deletion (utility of past retrievals after n retrievals); Annapureddy 2026 hindsight regret (precision 0.93 hard); Chen and Cheng 2026 label-fitted weights (reliability 0.64, emotion 0.55, self 0.23, goal 0.00).
limits: Absence of evidence after a truncated search; should be rechecked when search quota returns.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 6 remain open; the direct test is a cheap own experiment (log tags at write time, count later retrievals that changed an answer).

source: Theta-tagging study (2026), re-read for strength and surprise signals
finding: Tag signal was learning-time 3-8 Hz theta, linked to sleep-specific consolidation. The paper's peer reviewers asked for a control showing theta reflects a sleep-specific tag rather than general encoding strength. The authors guess weak neutral stimuli give only weak tags.
numbers: N=31 (from a18/b16): sleep advantage d=0.45; classifier cluster p=.010, d=0.72; theta predicts SO-spindle coupling, which predicts post-sleep memory. Surprise and effort are not measured.
limits: Scalp EEG, one paradigm, word-pair/associative memory, review comments show the encoding-strength confound is not excluded.
agent_relevance: Confirms no surprise or effort signal tested in humans for this purpose. Agent analogues (surprise, effort) remain untested; log them and test.

source: Search status: no pooled effect size and no pre-registered multi-lab test of test expectancy x sleep
finding: Europe PMC title and abstract searches for meta-analysis, test expectancy, future relevance and sleep found only: Wilhelm 2011, Wamsley 2016, Davidson 2021 review, Ashton and Cairney 2021, Reinhold 2026 (emotional response, not memory fate), and a Hu 2020 meta-analysis of targeted memory reactivation (cueing, not relevance).
numbers: Hu, Cheng, Chiu and Paller (2020) TMR meta-analysis exists (PMC7144680) but concerns cueing during sleep, not expected-relevance instructions.
limits: Search keyword dependent; preprint servers and unpublished nulls not searched.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open except for the rough pool in d02.
